case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court of appeals must review de novo (rather than for substantial evidence) the agency’s determination that specific threats and physical mistreatment do not amount to “persecution” for asylum eligibility.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (definition of “refugee,” incorporating “persecution”); and the INA’s judicial-review provisions governing standards of review for agency findings (including the substantial-evidence standard traditionally applied to factual findings in immigration cases).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the agency’s conclusion that the harm Urias-Orellana suffered in El Salvador did not rise to “persecution” is not a pure factfinding but a mixed question of applying a legal standard (“persecution”) to established facts, and that Congress did not clearly require substantial-evidence deference for this particular asylum-eligibility application; accordingly, courts should review the persecution determination de novo (at least where the dispute is chiefly about the legal threshold and comparability to other cases), which would promote uniformity and constrain under-protective agency decisionmaking, especially where credible death threats and physical mistreatment are involved.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues the court of appeals correctly applied substantial-evidence review because the persecution determination here is primarily factual—an assessment of degree, severity, and context of harm—and Congress, including through IIRIRA’s design, embraced deferential review for such determinations to promote uniformity and efficiency; de novo review is reserved for genuine legal questions such as the meaning of “persecution” as a definition, but once the standard is set, whether particular mistreatment crosses the line is a factbound judgment reviewed for substantial evidence (consistent with longstanding practice and cases like Elias-Zacarias).

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that, under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, some mixed questions count as “questions of law” and can trigger de novo review. But as Justice Barrett persuasively frames it, Wilkinson directs us to ask what the “primary work” is, and here the persecution-threshold determination is overwhelmingly a degree-and-context judgment about severity on a particular record—precisely the kind of call Congress channeled into substantial-evidence review in § 1252(b)(4)(B). Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces my institutional view: treating every persecution line-drawing as de novo would effectively circumvent § 1252(b)(4)(B) and unsettle the INA’s review structure absent a clear textual directive. We can hold narrowly that de novo review remains for genuine legal-standard errors (what “persecution” means or categorical misapplications), while record-specific threshold determinations are reviewed for whether the evidence compels the opposite conclusion under Elias-Zacarias.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that applying the legal standard of “persecution” to settled facts is a mixed question, and Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson sometimes treat such issues as “questions of law” reviewed de novo. But, as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Wilkinson turns on what does the “primary work,” and here the inquiry is overwhelmingly degree-and-context line-drawing—precisely the kind of factbound assessment Congress insulated in § 1252(b)(4)(B) by making administrative findings “conclusive” absent a record that compels the contrary. Nothing in Guerrero-Lasprilla purports to override that specific statutory command, and Elias-Zacarias confirms that courts may not reweigh asylum-eligibility inferences under a de novo label once the governing legal meaning is settled. De novo review remains available for genuine legal errors about the definition of “persecution,” but not for second-guessing the agency’s severity judgment on this record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument is that the persecution determination is a mixed question and thus a reviewable “question of law” under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, but Wilkinson’s “primary work” framework cuts against them here: this is predominantly a degree-and-context judgment about severity on a particular record. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 1252(b)(4)(B) is an explicit congressional instruction that factfinding and fact-intensive applications are conclusive unless the record compels the contrary result, and de novo review would invite routine reweighing of harms. Elias-Zacarias confirms that courts may not second-guess the agency’s asylum eligibility line-drawing absent compulsion, and nothing in Guerrero-Lasprilla displaces that specific statutory command. De novo review remains available for genuine legal errors about what “persecution” means, but not for disagreements with the agency’s case-specific severity assessment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that “persecution” is a legal standard and, under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, some mixed questions can warrant de novo review—but those cases themselves turn on what the “primary work” is. As Justice Barrett persuasively frames it, this determination is usually degree-and-context line-drawing about severity and inference from the record, which fits Congress’s instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) to treat agency factfinding as conclusive unless the record compels the opposite result. Justice Kagan’s workability concern reinforces that recharacterizing these threshold calls as de novo would invite appellate reweighing contrary to Elias-Zacarias, while still leaving room for de novo correction when the agency uses the wrong legal framework or an improper categorical rule. Given my focus on vulnerable asylum seekers, I would police legal-standard errors aggressively, but I do not see a justification for converting fact-dominated applications into de novo review in the face of Congress’s express substantial-evidence regime.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that “persecution” is a legal term and, under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, some mixed questions fall within “questions of law” for de novo review; that argument has force as a matter of uniformity. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Wilkinson’s “primary work” inquiry matters, and here the primary work is assessing severity, context, and degree on this record—precisely the kind of determination Congress insulated through § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s substantial-evidence/“record compels” regime. Elias-Zacarias fits that statutory design by preventing courts from relabeling factbound line-drawing as law simply because the legal standard is phrased in general terms. Loper Bright affects deference to agency legal interpretations, but it does not license us to dilute an express congressional command about review of factfinding and predominantly factual applications.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that whether established harms amount to “persecution” can be styled a mixed question, and Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson sometimes treat mixed questions as “questions of law.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, Wilkinson’s “primary work” inquiry matters: once the legal meaning of “persecution” is fixed, the remaining task is degree-and-context line drawing on a case-specific record, which fits § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s command that agency factfinding is conclusive absent compulsion to the contrary. Loper Bright strengthens judicial responsibility to say what “persecution” means, yet it does not license relabeling fact-intensive applications as “law” to circumvent Congress’s express substantial-evidence regime. Consistent with Elias-Zacarias, de novo review remains available for genuine legal-standard errors, not for reweighing whether this record crosses a severity threshold.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—that “persecution” is a legal standard and thus its application is a mixed question potentially reviewable de novo under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson—does not overcome the INA’s specific instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that agency fact findings are conclusive unless the record compels the opposite. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively frame it, Wilkinson’s “primary work” test cuts against de novo review here because the threshold determination is dominated by degree, severity, and contextual inferences—classic substantial-evidence territory under Elias-Zacarias. De novo review remains available for genuine legal errors about the definition of “persecution” or categorical misrules, but not for reweighing this record’s severity assessment. Recasting these determinations as de novo would be a major, impractical disruption of IIRIRA’s settled review structure without clear textual warrant, raising institutional and administrability concerns.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point is that “persecution” is a legal term and, under Guerrero-Lasprilla, some mixed questions fall within “questions of law” eligible for de novo review. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, § 1252(b)(4)(B) is a specific textual instruction that agency factfinding is conclusive unless the record compels the contrary, and Wilkinson’s “primary work” framework supports treating the persecution-threshold call—when the governing definition is undisputed—as predominantly fact-bound line-drawing about degree and context. Elias-Zacarias reinforces that courts may not reweigh those fact-intensive inferences absent compulsion, while preserving de novo review for genuine legal errors about what “persecution” means or for categorical misrules masquerading as “facts,” a point Justice Sotomayor rightly flags. Nothing in Guerrero-Lasprilla or Wilkinson authorizes courts to relabel this kind of severity assessment as “law” in a way that would sidestep Congress’s express substantial-evidence regime.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—that applying the legal term “persecution” is a mixed question reviewable de novo under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson—has force, because uniform legal standards matter and courts must be able to correct agencies that effectively narrow the law. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan stress, Wilkinson’s “primary work” inquiry matters: in the run of cases, the persecution-threshold call turns on degree, context, and severity inferences, which Congress instructed courts to review deferentially in § 1252(b)(4)(B) unless the record compels the contrary. Elias-Zacarias reinforces my pragmatic concern that recharacterizing these record-specific severity judgments as de novo invites appellate reweighing and destabilizes the INA’s review structure without a clear textual signal. I would preserve de novo review for genuine legal errors (wrong definition, categorical rule, failure to consider cumulative harm), but absent that, substantial-evidence review is the administrable and congressionally directed default.

John Roberts.reasoning: Congress directed that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s determination whether particular threats and mistreatment rise to the level of “persecution” typically turns on degree, severity, and context—work that is predominantly factual. Consistent with longstanding immigration practice and INS v. Elias-Zacarias, courts of appeals should apply substantial-evidence review to that factbound application of an accepted legal standard, while reserving de novo review for genuine legal questions about the meaning of “persecution” or legal error in the agency’s framework. Treating every “persecution” threshold call as de novo would risk a broad, destabilizing shift in INA review that Congress did not clearly authorize, undermining administrability and institutional legitimacy. A narrow holding affirming substantial-evidence review for the persecution determination (absent a claimed legal-standard error) best fits the statute and preserves precedent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s text directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s determination whether particular threats and mistreatment rise to the level of “persecution” is a fact-intensive judgment about degree, severity, and context. Nothing in § 1101(a)(42)(A)’s definition of “refugee” or in § 1252’s review provisions carves out “persecution” determinations for de novo review once the legal meaning of the term is settled. This Court’s longstanding practice in asylum eligibility disputes applies substantial-evidence review to such determinations, as reflected in INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), which emphasized that reversal is proper only when the record compels a contrary conclusion. Consistent with Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, courts may decide de novo the legal meaning of “persecution,” but the application of that standard to a particular record remains primarily factual and thus reviewed deferentially under § 1252(b)(4)(B).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and the determination whether particular threats and mistreatment cross the line into “persecution” is a fact-intensive assessment of degree and context that fits comfortably within that deferential framework. INS v. Elias-Zacarias confirms that an asylum ineligibility determination must be upheld if supported by “reasonable, substantial, and probative evidence,” and later cases (e.g., Ming Dai and Nasrallah) treat past-persecution and fear-of-persecution determinations as factual for purposes of review under § 1252(b)(4)(B). Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson do not compel de novo review here because they address reviewability of legal or mixed questions in different settings and do not displace Congress’s express command of substantial-evidence deference for factbound determinations central to asylum eligibility. De novo review remains available for the purely legal meaning of “persecution,” but once the standard is settled, applying it to an applicant’s particular experiences is reviewed for substantial evidence.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The INA’s review provision directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and whether particular threats and mistreatment cross the line into “persecution” is a degree-and-context judgment that is primarily factual rather than a pure legal interpretation. INS v. Elias-Zacarias reinforces that courts may not reweigh the record in asylum eligibility disputes and must apply substantial-evidence review to the agency’s factbound inferences about the severity and character of harm. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson recognize that some mixed questions can be treated as “questions of law,” but they also emphasize context; here Congress legislated against a settled background of deferential review in asylum eligibility determinations, and nothing in the text clearly displaces § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s command. Courts still retain de novo authority to clarify the legal meaning of “persecution” as a standard, but once that standard is set, application to a particular record remains for substantial-evidence review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The INA’s review scheme, including 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s command that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” points toward deferential review where the agency is making a degree-and-context judgment about the severity of harm. INS v. Elias-Zacarias reinforces that courts overturn asylum-eligibility determinations only when the record compels the opposite conclusion, and its reasoning treats the application of the asylum standard to case-specific circumstances as a domain for substantial-evidence review rather than de novo second-guessing. Guerrero-Lasprilla (and Wilkinson) recognize de novo review for certain “questions of law” that are mixed questions, but here the dispute is less about the meaning of “persecution” in § 1101(a)(42)(A) and more about whether particular threats and mistreatment cross a factbound threshold—an inquiry where workability and statutory coherence favor the traditional substantial-evidence framework. Loper Bright’s rejection of Chevron deference does not alter Congress’s chosen standard of judicial review for agency factfinding and fact-intensive applications under § 1252.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s review provision draws a clear textual line: “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary.” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B). Once the legal meaning of “persecution” in § 1101(a)(42)(A) is fixed, deciding whether a particular episode of threats and mistreatment crosses that line is an intensely factbound, degree-and-context judgment that fits comfortably within Congress’s command of deferential review, consistent with INS v. Elias-Zacarias’s articulation of substantial-evidence review in asylum eligibility disputes. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson confirm that some mixed questions may be reviewed de novo when they are primarily legal, but this one—evaluating severity and lived experience in context—is primarily factual, and nothing in the statute clearly displaces the long-settled substantial-evidence approach. Loper Bright reinforces that courts decide legal questions independently, but it does not authorize recharacterizing a fact-intensive “line-drawing” application as a legal question to evade § 1252(b)(4)(B).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and this Court has long treated core asylum-eligibility determinations as factbound applications reviewed under substantial-evidence principles. INS v. Elias-Zacarias underscores that where the agency is drawing inferences and making degree-and-context judgments about persecution-related elements, the court of appeals may reverse only if the record compels the opposite result, not simply because it would decide the issue differently. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson preserve de novo review for genuine “questions of law,” including misinterpretation of the legal standard, but they do not require de novo review of the agency’s fact-intensive assessment of whether particular threats and mistreatment cross the persecution line. A de novo regime would be a significant and impractical shift from IIRIRA’s deferential review structure and would invite appellate relitigation of heavily case-specific severity determinations, undermining administrability and the settled balance Congress chose.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review scheme directs courts to treat the agency’s determinations of what occurred and how severe it was as findings reviewed under the substantial-evidence standard, and the “persecution” line-drawing here is predominantly that kind of factbound severity assessment rather than a dispute over the legal meaning of “persecution” in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A). INS v. Elias-Zacarias applied substantial-evidence review to the BIA’s asylum ineligibility determination and reflects Congress’s choice—carried forward into IIRIRA’s review provisions—that courts not conduct de novo reweighing of the record in asylum eligibility adjudications. Consistent with Wilkinson v. Garland, mixed questions are reviewed deferentially when the “primary work” is factual application rather than pure legal interpretation; de novo review remains available only for genuine legal questions about the definition of “persecution” itself. Guerrero-Lasprilla does not compel de novo review here because it involved a statutory “questions of law” carveout and a primarily legal inquiry (equitable tolling), unlike the degree-of-harm assessment at issue.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s determination whether particular threats and mistreatment cross the line into “persecution” is, in context, a degree-and-circumstances judgment that is primarily factual and therefore reviewed for substantial evidence. INS v. Elias-Zacarias reflects the longstanding approach in asylum cases: once the legal meaning of the standard is set, the application to a record is reviewed deferentially unless the evidence compels the opposite conclusion. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson confirm that mixed questions are not categorically de novo under the INA; rather, the standard turns on whether the issue is primarily legal or primarily factual, and this one is the latter. Preserving deferential review here promotes procedural regularity and efficient adjudication, while leaving room for de novo correction when a court identifies an erroneous legal definition of “persecution.”

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court of appeals must review de novo (rather than for substantial evidence) the agency’s determination that the petitioner’s alleged threats and physical mistreatment in El Salvador did not amount to “persecution” for asylum purposes.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (definition of “refugee,” incorporating the persecution requirement) and the INA’s judicial-review provisions governing review of agency determinations (as argued by the parties in relation to substantial-evidence vs. de novo review).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that whether established facts rise to the legal standard of “persecution” is a mixed question of law and fact that—under the INA’s text and structure—should receive de novo review (at least for mixed questions resembling asylum-eligibility determinations), and that the First Circuit erred by treating the persecution determination as essentially factual and applying substantial-evidence review; they contend this misallocation of the standard of review risks systematic under-recognition of persecution (including credible death threats) and inconsistent legal rules across circuits and the agency.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues the court of appeals correctly applied substantial-evidence review because the ‘persecution’ determination is predominantly factual in this posture (a fact-bound application of a settled legal standard to a particular record), Congress in IIRIRA channeled and limited judicial reweighing of asylum records, and longstanding practice—including this Court’s asylum cases—treats persecution/eligibility determinations as subject to deferential review; the government concedes that purely legal questions about the meaning of the term “persecution” remain reviewable de novo, but maintains that this case presents only a deferentially reviewed application of law to facts.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest point from the other side: § 1252(b)(4)(B) expressly makes conclusive only “findings of fact,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla confirms that some applications of law to settled facts can be “questions of law.” But Wilkinson, as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, directs us to calibrate review of mixed questions based on whether the inquiry is predominantly legal or predominantly factual; the ordinary “persecution” call is a severity-and-context characterization of a particular record that functions chiefly as a factual judgment within the Elias-Zacarias substantial-evidence framework. The narrow, text-respecting way to reconcile these cases is to preserve de novo review for genuine interpretive disputes about the meaning of “persecution” or misstatements of the standard, while applying substantial-evidence review to this record-bound application so courts of appeals do not reweigh harms under the guise of ‘law.’ That approach is minimalist, maintains institutional legitimacy by keeping appellate courts in their proper reviewing role, and avoids reading Guerrero-Lasprilla’s jurisdiction-restoration holding to silently transform routine asylum eligibility assessments into de novo review.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett raise the strongest textual point that § 1252(b)(4)(B) makes conclusive only “findings of fact,” and they invoke Guerrero-Lasprilla to argue that applying “persecution” to settled facts is therefore a reviewable “question of law.” But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh explain, Wilkinson confirms that the applicable standard of review for mixed questions depends on whether the inquiry is predominantly factual, and the ordinary asylum “persecution” determination is a record-characterization judgment about severity and context—functionally adjacent to factfinding—rather than a dispute over the meaning of the statutory term. Guerrero-Lasprilla arose in a jurisdiction-restoration setting and cannot be read to displace Congress’s conclusive-effect regime or Elias-Zacarias’s substantial-evidence framework for these fact-bound determinations absent a genuine interpretive disagreement about what “persecution” means. De novo review remains appropriate where the agency misstated the legal definition, but not where the quarrel is simply whether this record crosses a fact-intensive threshold.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett press the best textual point—that § 1252(b)(4)(B) makes conclusive only “administrative findings of fact,” so we should not casually treat legal sufficiency as factfinding—but that does not itself establish a de novo standard for the ultimate persecution determination. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh explain, Wilkinson teaches that even when a matter is called “mixed,” the proper standard of review may remain deferential where the inquiry is predominantly factual; the persecution call in ordinary asylum cases is a severity-and-context characterization of a particular record, and de novo review would predictably become appellate reweighing. Guerrero-Lasprilla’s “questions of law” discussion (emphasized by Justice Sotomayor) arose in the § 1252(a)(2)(D) jurisdiction-restoration context and should not be read to silently displace the long-settled substantial-evidence framework reflected in Elias-Zacarias and codified in Congress’s compelled-to-conclude language. I would preserve de novo review where the agency misstated the governing definition of “persecution,” but not convert this recurring, fact-dominant application into a broadly de novo inquiry.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is administrability under Wilkinson—persecution determinations are often “severity-and-context” judgments that look predominantly factual, and substantial-evidence review avoids appellate reweighing. But that functional concern cannot override the textual line Congress drew in § 1252(b)(4)(B): it renders conclusive only “findings of fact,” and—consistent with Guerrero-Lasprilla—the legal sufficiency of settled facts to meet a statutory threshold remains a question of law, even if fact-sensitive. Elias-Zacarias, as Justice Thomas emphasizes, demands deference to agency factfinding and non-compelled inferences (especially motive), yet it does not clearly require deference on the ultimate legal adequacy of harm as “persecution,” and treating that step as effectively unreviewable risks systemic under-recognition of serious harm. I would preserve robust deference on true factual disputes while insisting on independent judicial judgment over the statutory threshold to promote uniformity and protect vulnerable applicants.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch make the best textual push: § 1252(b)(4)(B) by its terms makes conclusive only “findings of fact,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla confirms that application-of-law-to-settled-facts can qualify as a “question of law” in the INA. But Wilkinson’s framework, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, is not a relabeling exercise; it directs us to decide the standard of review for a mixed question by asking whether the inquiry is predominantly legal or predominantly factual, and the ordinary persecution determination is a record-specific severity-and-context characterization that functions like factfinding. Read that way, we preserve de novo review for the meaning of “persecution” (and for legal misstatements) while keeping substantial-evidence review for this fact-dominant application, consistent with Elias-Zacarias and Congress’s channeling design without turning courts of appeals into reweighers of hard records. I do not see Guerrero-Lasprilla—arising in § 1252(a)(2)(D)’s jurisdiction-restoration context—as clearly commanding de novo review of routine persecution calls where no interpretive dispute about the statutory standard is presented.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s (and Justice Kavanaugh’s) strongest point is administrability: persecution determinations are severity-and-context judgments that look “primarily factual” under Wilkinson, so substantial-evidence review purportedly prevents appellate reweighing. But under the text Congress wrote, § 1252(b)(4)(B) makes conclusive only “administrative findings of fact,” and that phrase cannot be expanded—based on prudential concerns— to include the distinct legal sufficiency question whether established facts meet Congress’s statutory threshold of “persecution.” Wilkinson’s “primarily factual” framing may counsel restraint in how courts conduct de novo review, yet it does not authorize reclassifying the application of a legal standard as factfinding; and Guerrero-Lasprilla confirms, within the INA, that applying a legal standard to settled facts can be a “question of law.” Elias-Zacarias still does important work by demanding deference to factfinding and non-compelled inferences, but it does not clearly command deference on the legal side of the mixed question, and post–Loper Bright I see no clear congressional instruction to cede that judicial function to the agency.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett make the strongest point that § 1252(b)(4)(B) expressly renders conclusive only “findings of fact,” and Guerrero-Lasprilla confirms that some applications of law to settled facts qualify as “questions of law.” But Wilkinson, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, directs us to ask whether the mixed question is predominantly legal or predominantly factual, and the “persecution” line in ordinary asylum cases is a severity-and-context characterization that operates much closer to the substantial-evidence model codified in § 1252(b)(4)(B) and reflected in Elias-Zacarias than to a freestanding interpretive dispute. I agree (with Justice Barrett) that courts must decide the meaning of “persecution” de novo, yet that does not entail de novo reweighing of whether this record crosses the line absent a misstatement of the governing definition. Institutionally, treating these routine, record-bound determinations as de novo “legal questions” would predictably expand appellate second-guessing in a way Congress’s channeling scheme and our settled practice counsel against.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is administrability under Wilkinson—many “persecution” determinations are severity-and-context characterizations that feel factbound—but that functional instinct cannot expand § 1252(b)(4)(B) beyond its textual limit of “administrative findings of fact.” Even accepting Wilkinson’s “primarily factual” gloss for some mixed questions, it does not license treating the legal sufficiency step (whether undisputed harms meet Congress’s statutory threshold) as a conclusive factfinding; that move risks collapsing the law/fact distinction Congress chose. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Elias-Zacarias and settled practice underscores the need to avoid appellate reweighing, and I agree courts must defer to historical facts and non-compelled inferences, but Elias-Zacarias does not clearly require deference on the ultimate legal adequacy of harm as “persecution.” Guerrero-Lasprilla, though arising in a jurisdictional provision, reinforces that application-of-law-to-fact can be a “question of law” under the INA, and post–Loper Bright I do not see a clearer statutory command than § 1252(b)(4)(B) to make that legal application conclusively agency-controlled.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is textual: § 1252(b)(4)(B) makes conclusive only “findings of fact,” so courts should not evade that by calling legal sufficiency “fact.” But Wilkinson, as the Chief Justice emphasizes, supplies the missing link: even when an issue is a mixed question, the proper review depends on whether it is predominantly legal or factual, and the persecution call on a settled definition is usually a record-specific severity-and-context characterization that functions like factfinding in practice. Guerrero-Lasprilla prevents us from insulating genuine legal errors—e.g., a misconstruction of “persecution” or an incorrect legal yardstick—but it does not require de novo reweighing of whether this particular record crosses the line absent such an error. This approach preserves procedural fairness (correct law applied, reasons given) while respecting Congress’s channeling design and Elias-Zacarias’s warning against appellate second-guessing unless the record compels the contrary conclusion.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(4)(B) provides that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and in the ordinary asylum case the agency’s determination whether record mistreatment rises to “persecution” is a highly fact-bound application of a settled standard that fits comfortably within deferential substantial-evidence review. Our practice in asylum cases—exemplified by INS v. Elias-Zacarias—has treated eligibility determinations turning on the record as reviewed for substantial evidence, and nothing in IIRIRA suggests Congress silently displaced that approach in favor of across-the-board de novo review for this kind of application-to-facts issue. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson confirm that some “mixed questions” can be reviewed as “questions of law,” but they also recognize that where the inquiry is predominantly factual, deference remains appropriate; this case presents that latter posture. A narrow holding preserving de novo review for pure legal questions about the meaning of “persecution,” while applying substantial-evidence review to the agency’s fact-intensive application here, best respects precedent, Congress’s channeling of judicial review, and the institutional need for administrable standards.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review text, particularly 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), directs that "administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary," and in this posture the agency’s determination that the petitioner’s mistreatment did not rise to the level of "persecution" is best understood as a fact-bound application of a settled standard to a particular record rather than an interpretation of statutory meaning. INS v. Elias-Zacarias reflects the longstanding understanding that asylum-eligibility determinations are reviewed deferentially, and nothing in § 1101(a)(42)(A) or IIRIRA’s channeling of review clearly displaces that approach for these record-intensive assessments. Consistent with Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, purely legal questions about the meaning of "persecution" remain reviewable de novo, but where—as here—the dispute is whether particular harms meet an accepted legal threshold, substantial-evidence review is the proper, textually anchored standard. The petitioners’ request for de novo review would invite appellate reweighing of asylum records in tension with Congress’s limits on judicial second-guessing embodied in § 1252(b)(4)(B).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and the agency’s determination whether a particular set of threats and mistreatment rises to “persecution” is, in this posture, a highly fact-bound application of a settled standard rather than a dispute about the legal meaning of the term. INS v. Elias-Zacarias reflects this Court’s consistent approach of applying substantial-evidence deference to the agency’s asylum-eligibility determinations, and nothing in IIRIRA suggests Congress silently invited courts of appeals to reweigh persecution determinations de novo. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson confirm that some “questions of law” include mixed questions, but they also recognize that when the inquiry is predominantly factual, deferential review remains appropriate; de novo review is reserved for genuine interpretive questions about what “persecution” means, which the government concedes are still reviewable de novo. Requiring de novo review here would undermine Congress’s channeling of immigration adjudication to the agency and risk turning courts of appeals into record-reweighers in asylum cases, with significant practical consequences for enforcement and finality.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The INA’s text makes agency “findings of fact” conclusive unless a reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude otherwise, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), but that cabined deference does not by its terms extend to mixed questions about whether undisputed or established facts satisfy the statutory standard of “persecution” under § 1101(a)(42)(A). Under Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, the Court has treated the application of a legal standard to established facts as a “question of law” for INA judicial-review purposes, and Wilkinson v. Garland reinforces that mixed questions can require meaningful appellate review beyond pure fact deference. De novo review of the persecution determination better promotes uniformity and prevents systematic under-recognition of severe harms—like credible death threats—where vulnerable asylum seekers bear the consequences of overly deferential review. The government’s reliance on INS v. Elias-Zacarias and IIRIRA’s general channeling of review cannot override the statute’s text limiting substantial-evidence deference to factual findings rather than the ultimate legal characterization of those facts as “persecution.”

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review scheme, read in light of IIRIRA’s channeling of review and this Court’s settled asylum practice, most naturally treats whether a particular record amounts to “persecution” as a predominantly fact-bound application of a settled standard, reviewed under the substantial-evidence rule rather than de novo. INS v. Elias-Zacarias applied that deferential framework to asylum-eligibility determinations, and nothing in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) or the INA’s review provisions clearly displaces it for persecution findings as opposed to pure questions about the meaning of “persecution.” Guerrero-Lasprilla confirms that some “application-of-law-to-fact” issues can count as legal questions in certain INA provisions, but it does not compel de novo review where the inquiry turns mainly on weighing and characterizing a particular evidentiary record, as Wilkinson likewise underscores in distinguishing primarily factual mixed questions. Post–Loper Bright, courts still decide statutory meaning de novo, but here the government concedes de novo review for that kind of interpretive dispute; this case instead concerns the agency’s fact-intensive determination on the established record, appropriately reviewed for substantial evidence.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(4)(B) by its terms makes conclusive only “administrative findings of fact” unless “any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and it does not extend that deferential standard to the legal application of the statutory term “persecution” to undisputed or established facts. Consistent with Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr and Wilkinson v. Garland, the INA’s use of “questions of law” encompasses mixed questions, and while those cases addressed jurisdiction under § 1252(a)(2)(D), their reasoning underscores that applying a legal standard to facts is not itself a “finding of fact” covered by § 1252(b)(4)(B). INS v. Elias-Zacarias confirms deference for factual findings (and codified language later appears in § 1252(b)(4)(B)), but it does not authorize courts to treat a legal threshold like “persecution” as a factual finding immune from de novo review. In light of separation-of-powers concerns after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, courts should say what the law is—including whether found facts meet Congress’s statutory standard—while still deferring on genuinely factual determinations.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), directs that “administrative findings of fact” are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude otherwise, and the agency’s determination whether particular threats and mistreatment amount to “persecution” is typically a highly fact-bound application of a settled standard to a specific record. Consistent with INS v. Elias-Zacarias, courts have long treated core asylum-eligibility determinations resting on record inferences as subject to substantial-evidence review rather than plenary reweighing, which also accords with IIRIRA’s channeling of judicial review and practical workability concerns. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson recognize that some mixed questions can be “questions of law” for jurisdictional purposes, but they do not require de novo review across the board where the dispute is predominantly factual in nature. Courts may still review de novo any genuine legal dispute about the meaning of “persecution,” but on this record the First Circuit did not err by applying deferential review to the agency’s case-specific assessment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The INA’s text specifies a deferential standard only for “administrative findings of fact,” making them “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B); it does not prescribe deference for the application of a legal standard to established facts. Under Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, the INA’s reference to “questions of law” encompasses mixed questions of law and fact, so whether proven threats and mistreatment satisfy the legal standard of “persecution” is at least reviewable de novo insofar as it turns on applying the statutory term to found facts. INS v. Elias-Zacarias is best read as applying substantial-evidence review to underlying factual determinations (and the agency’s finding that the record did not compel the petitioner’s asserted inference), not as a holding that the ultimate persecution/eligibility determination is always insulated from independent judicial judgment. And after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, absent a clear statutory command for deference on legal questions, courts should apply their own judgment to the legal component of the persecution inquiry while respecting § 1252(b)(4)(B) for pure factfinding.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under the INA’s judicial-review framework, the agency’s application of the settled “persecution” standard to a particular evidentiary record is predominantly fact-bound and thus reviewed for substantial evidence rather than de novo. Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr confirms that certain mixed questions can qualify as “questions of law” for jurisdictional purposes, but Wilkinson v. Garland underscores that the standard of appellate review still turns on whether the mixed question is primarily legal or primarily factual—here, it largely entails weighing the severity and context of threats and mistreatment. Consistent with INS v. Elias-Zacarias and the longstanding IIRIRA-era practice of deferential review of asylum eligibility determinations, courts remain free to correct de novo any legal misdefinition of “persecution,” but should not reweigh record facts under a de novo label.
